newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Minister sees Russia-IMF 1997 agreement in April.
newsitem.headline: Minister sees Russia-IMF 1997 agreement in April.

text.p: A deal between Russia and the International Monetary Fund detailing economic plans for 1997 could be signed next month, a senior Russian minister was quoted as saying on Monday.

But Interfax news agency quoted Yevgeny Yasin, minister in charge of Russian economic stratgey, as saying that he did not think the deal could be signed during this week's visit to Moscow by IMF managing director Michel Camdessus.

Camdessus arrives in Moscow on Monday afternoon for three days of talks with senior officials, including President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. He will address students on Wednesday and give a news conference on Thursday.
Yasin said Russia's problems on tax collection and restructuring the economy would be among the toughest issues on Camdessus' agenda.
The IMF has already delayed several tranches of its $10 billion three-year loan to Russia because of poor tax receipts and officials from both sides are working on a statement of intent for 1997.

Russia's newly reshuffled government has also targeted the county's powerful natural monopolies, including natural gas giant Gazprom and electric company UES, for restructuring in an effort to revive flagging economic reforms.
Yasin said ministers had already drawn up a draft resolution on reforming natural monopolies, most of them in the energy and transportation sectors.
He said the IMF loan was important for the success of Russia's existing and future Eurobond issues, as well as for its bid to join the Paris Club of creditor countries.
Russia, which inherited responsibility for the debts of the former Soviet Union, has reached deals with the Paris Club to reschedule these debts.
Moscow is now seeking membership of the Paris Club as a creditor, hoping this will make it easier to recover loans extended by the Soviet Union to a host of Third World countries.

Chubais, recently appointed to spearhead the government's renewed economic reform efforts, has said the IMF loan was declining in importance for Russia, although it remained a significant lure for much-needed foreign investment.
